hints.title: Find the possible partners
hints.body: For a term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, its partner would be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>74</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. List the distinct pairs for which both terms belong to the given arithmetic sequence.
hints.recap: The terms have common difference <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, so membership can be checked from the first term.
hints.pitfall: A proposed partner may fall outside the sequence.
hints.pause: Build a list of valid pairs without counting a pair twice.

recall.reminder: Use the first term and common difference to describe the finite arithmetic sequence.

hints.title: Check the exceptional terms
hints.body: Identify any terms that are not in a valid pair. Remember that the problem asks for two distinct terms.
hints.recap: A term equal to its own proposed partner cannot form a pair with itself here.
hints.pitfall: Do not silently discard a term that can be selected without creating a valid pair.
hints.pause: Decide which unpaired terms can be added to a pair-avoiding selection.

recall.reminder: Separate complementary pairs from exceptional unpaired objects.

hints.title: Prove both the bound and its sharpness
hints.body: A selection avoiding a valid pair can take at most one member from each pair. Combine that restriction with the exceptional terms, and construct a selection attaining your bound.
hints.recap: The first forced size is just beyond the largest possible avoiding selection.
hints.pitfall: A bound alone is not enough: show that a smaller selection really can avoid the required event.
hints.pause: Count the largest avoiding selection and prove that adding one more chosen term must create a pair.

recall.reminder: Find the largest configuration that avoids the event, then force it beyond that size.

solution:
There are 24 terms. The valid pairs are (4,70),(7,67),…,(34,40), giving 11 disjoint pairs. The term 1 has no partner in the list, and 37 cannot pair with itself because the terms must be distinct.

A selection with no required pair therefore contains at most 11+2=13 terms. This is attainable by selecting one term from each pair together with 1 and 37.

Any selection of 14 terms must contain both members of at least one pair. The smallest forcing value is 14. Answer: C.
knowledgePattern: Maximise a selection avoiding complementary pairs, then force a pair
